section.title: Pressing Toward the Goal
section.sectionRationale: Having renounced his own righteousness, Paul makes clear he has not yet arrived. Like a runner he forgets what lies behind and strains toward the prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ. He calls the mature to the same mind, warns with tears against those whose god is their belly and whose minds are on earthly things, and lifts the church's eyes to their true citizenship in heaven, from which they await the Savior who will transform their lowly bodies.
section.thesis: Not yet perfected, Paul presses on like a runner toward the prize of God's upward call in Christ, urging the mature to the same pursuit and to follow his example, warning with tears against enemies of the cross whose minds are set on earthly things, and anchoring hope in a citizenship in heaven from which the Savior will come to transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.
section.frameNote: Three movements: pressing on toward the goal, not having yet arrived; the call to follow the pattern, weeping over the enemies of the cross; and the hope of heavenly citizenship and the Savior who transforms our bodies, so stand firm.

units.label: Pressing on toward the goal
units.note: forgetting what is behind, straining ahead

verses.text: Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already been made perfect, but I {{dioko|press on}} to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me.
Brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead,
I press on toward the goal to win the {{brabeion|prize}} of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.

units.label: Follow the pattern, not the enemies of the cross
units.note: many walk as enemies of the cross

verses.text: All of us who are mature should embrace this point of view. And if you think differently about some issue, God will reveal this to you as well.
Nevertheless, we must live up to what we have already attained.
Join one another in following my example, brothers, and carefully observe those who walk according to the pattern we set for you.
For as I have often told you before, and now say again even with tears: Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ.
Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Their minds are set on earthly things.

units.label: Citizenship in heaven
units.note: the Savior who transforms our bodies

verses.text: But our {{politeuma|citizenship}} is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ,
who, by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself, will {{metaschematizo|transform}} our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.
Therefore, my brothers, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, that is how you must {{steko|stand firm}} in the Lord, my beloved.

dioko.gloss: To pursue, to press on, to chase hard after, the word used for a runner straining for the finish or a hunter after prey. Paul admits he has not yet arrived, but he pursues Christ with everything, a picture of the Christian life as earnest, wholehearted, forward-moving pursuit, not passive drifting.

brabeion.gloss: The prize awarded to the victor in the games, the wreath given at the finish line. The prize Paul runs for is God's heavenly calling in Christ, the fullness of life with Him. It is not earned as wages but received at the end of the race God Himself has called us to run.

politeuma.gloss: Commonwealth, citizenship, the state to which one belongs. For a Roman colony that prized its citizenship, this word lands with force: the believer's true homeland is heaven, and its ruler is the Lord Jesus. Christians live as a colony of heaven awaiting their King, not as those whose minds are set on earthly things.

metaschematizo.gloss: To transform, to change the outward form. At His coming Christ will transform our lowly, mortal bodies to share the likeness of His own glorious, resurrected body. Salvation is not escape from the body but its redemption; the same power by which He rules all things will raise and glorify His people.

steko.gloss: To stand firm, to hold one's ground. In light of the coming Savior and the sure hope of glorified bodies, Paul calls his beloved church to stand fast in the Lord, immovable amid opposition and false teaching. Assurance of the goal is the ground of steadfastness now.

basic.context: Paul has just said knowing Christ is everything, and now he adds honesty: he has not yet arrived. He is like a runner who forgets the track behind and pours himself into the race ahead, straining for the prize of God's call. He urges the church to run the same way and to imitate him, and he weeps over people who live as enemies of the cross, whose appetites are their god. Then he lifts their gaze upward: our real citizenship is in heaven, and the Savior is coming to give us new, glorious bodies. So stand firm.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul balances two truths that can seem to pull apart: the believer's righteousness is a finished gift in Christ, yet the Christian life is a strenuous pursuit of maturity. Both are true. The athletic imagery teaches effort without earning, and the heavenly hope teaches perseverance grounded in certainty.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul says he does not coast but dioko, presses on hard, like a runner after the brabeion, the victor's prize, of God's heavenly call. Our politeuma, citizenship or commonwealth, is in heaven. From there the Savior will metaschematizo, transform, our lowly bodies. So we steko, stand firm, in the Lord.
basic.typology: The heavenly citizenship fulfills the pilgrim hope of Abraham, who looked for a city with foundations whose builder is God. The transformation of our lowly bodies into the likeness of Christ's glorious body fulfills the resurrection hope, with the risen Christ as the firstfruits and pattern of what His people will become.
basic.christ: Christ is the one who first took hold of Paul, the prize at the end of the race, the Savior awaited from heaven, and the pattern of the glorious body believers will share. His resurrection secures ours; the same power by which He subjects all things will raise and transform His people. He is the beginning, goal, and guarantee of the Christian's hope.
basic.god: God is the one who issues the heavenly calling that draws the runner forward, who reveals truth to the willing, and whose power in Christ will bring all things into subjection and raise His people. The whole race is run toward Him and by His enabling, and the certainty of the end rests on His power.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 9 pictures the Christian life as a race for an imperishable prize. 1 John 3:2 says we shall be like Him when He appears. Hebrews 11 describes the saints seeking a heavenly homeland.
basic.oneStory: God's people have always been pilgrims journeying toward a homeland they do not yet see. Paul runs that race toward the heavenly city and the coming King, and the story ends where it is heading here: the Savior returns, the dead are raised in glorious bodies like His, and the citizens of heaven stand at last in the presence of their Lord.

context.literary:
The passage begins in the middle of a thought, which is why it feels like a continuation and not a new start. Verses 10 and 11 ended on the hope of resurrection, and verse 12 immediately guards against a misreading: Paul does not claim to have reached it. The honest admission is followed by a two-step image, forgetting and straining, and then a finish line in verse 14.

The structure is a deliberate triad of contrasts. Verses 12 to 16 present the runner, the mature person who keeps going. Verses 17 to 19 set the example of Paul and his companions against the enemies of the cross. Verses 20 to 21 lift the whole picture to heaven and the coming of the Savior. Each section has its own dominant word. The first is pressing on, the second walking or living, and the third citizenship. Chapter 4 verse 1 then closes it with a call to stand firm, so that the section ends where a soldier stands, not where a runner finishes.

The passage is full of reversals. The verb Paul uses for pressing on, dioko, is the same verb as in verse 6 for persecuting the church, so the man who once chased believers now chases Christ. The ending of the enemies is destruction, and the end of the citizens is a transformed body. Their glory is in shame; His glory is the pattern for ours. Their minds are on earthly things; ours is a commonwealth in heaven. The pairs sit close together so that readers cannot miss the contrast.
context.historical:
Philippi was a Roman colony, with the privileges and pride of belonging to the empire, Acts 16:12. Colonists were citizens of Rome living far from Rome, and they kept Roman law, Roman custom and loyalty to the emperor in a place that was not Italy. The word Paul chooses in verse 20 would therefore have made immediate sense. A church of Philippians knew what it meant to belong to a capital they might never see, and to look to it for protection and rule. The title Savior, along with Lord, was used for the emperor, so Paul's claim that the Savior is coming from heaven would have sounded pointed to those who heard it in a Roman setting.

The athletic imagery fits the Greek and Roman world as well. Paul uses race and prize language elsewhere, 1 Corinthians 9:24 to 27 and 2 Timothy 4:7 to 8, and the Philippians would have known games of that kind.

The enemies of the cross were probably real and present, and Paul says he has told them about them often and now says so with tears. The picture of a god who is the belly would be recognizable in a city full of feasting and temple meals, but it could also point to those who stressed dietary rules. Either way the contrast with the suffering Paul describes in chapters 1 and 3 is sharp, and the church was living under pressure to decide which model to follow.
context.canonical:
The image of life as a journey toward a promised place runs through the whole Bible. Abraham was called to leave his country, Genesis 12:1, and called himself a foreigner and outsider when burying Sarah, Genesis 23:4. Jacob described his years as travels, Genesis 47:9, and the psalmist said he was a stranger like all his fathers, Psalm 39:12. Hebrews 11:13 to 16 gathers that tradition into a single paragraph, saying they were seeking a country of their own, and Hebrews 13:14 says believers have no permanent city here.

The warning against looking back echoes the wilderness generation, who longed for the food of Egypt, Numbers 11:5, and wanted to return there, Numbers 14:3 to 4. Jesus' blunt saying, Remember Lot's wife, Luke 17:32, warns of the same backward glance. Paul's forgetting is not amnesia; it is refusing to let the past dictate the pace of the present.

The heavenly citizenship is anticipated in Ephesians 2:19, where Gentiles are no longer foreigners but fellow citizens, and Colossians 3:1 to 4, where the believer's life is hidden with Christ in God. The transformation of the body is the great theme of 1 Corinthians 15:42 to 49, which uses language that is close to verse 21, and of 1 John 3:2, where believers will be like Him when He appears. Romans 8:23 speaks of the redemption of our bodies. Second Timothy 4:7 to 8 gives the same race and the same crown from the end of the road, and 1 Peter 5:4 calls it a crown of glory that will never fade.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to correct two opposite errors at once. One is complacency, the idea that because Christ has given righteousness the work is done. The other is anxiety, the sense that a believer must keep earning a place. His own example answers both. He is secure because Christ took hold of him, and he is restless because he has not yet arrived. The reader is meant to become dissatisfied in the right way.

He also gives the church people to follow. In verse 17 he asks them to copy him and to watch those who live as he does, because a pattern is easier to follow than a principle. The warning in verses 18 and 19 is delivered with tears, which tells us it is the love of a pastor and not the scorn of a critic. He wants them to see where a self-centred life ends.

The last section is meant to console. The Philippians were under pressure and some were suffering, 1:28 to 30. Paul reminds them where they belong and who is coming for them. Their present lowliness is not the last word, and so they can stand. The practical aim of the whole paragraph is the single command at the end, stand firm, and everything before it is the ground for that.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Verses 12 to 14 are Paul's personal testimony, and they function as an example more than a rule. The imperatives are in verses 15 to 17: embrace this view, live up to what has been attained, and follow the pattern. Verse 15's promise that God will reveal what is not yet clear is a description of how God deals with a mature community. Verse 17 says to observe those who walk in line with the apostles, which is a practical rule for choosing teachers and models. Verses 18 and 19 describe the enemies and do not authorize hostility toward them; Paul's response is weeping. Verses 20 and 21 are description of what is true and what is coming. They are not commands, and they are the reason for the final command. We should not take the athletic language to mean that salvation is a competition among believers; the prize is the same call to all, and runners help each other.

debates.question: If righteousness is a finished gift, why must Paul still press on?

views.label: Justification is complete, sanctification is a pursuit
views.case: Paul's right standing is settled in Christ, yet the Christian life is a race toward full maturity and final glory; effort is the fruit of grace, not a way to earn standing, since Christ first took hold of him.

views.label: Salvation is still uncertain and must be secured
views.case: Reading the pursuit as earning salvation contradicts chapter 3's gift of righteousness and 1:6; the striving is toward maturity and the prize, resting on Christ's prior grasp of us.

debates.bearing: The passage holds assurance and effort together: because Christ has taken hold of us, we press on toward the goal, running from grace, not for acceptance.

debates.question: What does transform our lowly bodies teach about the Christian hope?

views.label: Bodily resurrection and glorification
views.case: Christ will change our mortal bodies to be like His glorious resurrection body; the hope is redemption of the body, not escape from it, by the power that subjects all things to Him.

views.label: A purely spiritual, disembodied future
views.case: This misreads the text; Paul promises transformed bodies like Christ's risen body, affirming a physical resurrection, not a bodiless immortality.

debates.bearing: Christian hope is the resurrection and glorification of the body at Christ's return, grounded in His own risen body as the pattern and His power as the guarantee.

debates.question: Who are the enemies of the cross in verses 18 and 19?

views.label: Libertine professing Christians
views.case: A god who is the belly, a glory in shame and a mind on earthly things suit people who use grace as an excuse for indulgence. Paul weeps over them, which suggests they are inside or near the church, and Romans 16:18 describes false teachers serving their own appetites.

views.label: Judaizing teachers
views.case: The belly can point to food laws, and the shame to circumcision, which fits the warning that opens the chapter, 3:2. Galatians 6:12 to 14 also ties the same group to avoiding the offense of the cross.

views.label: A general type, not one party
views.case: Paul gives no name and only describes a way of living whose measure is the self. The portrait can cover both legalists and libertines, since each trusts something other than the cross.

debates.bearing: The ambiguity helps rather than hurts. What Paul wants the church to see is the shape, a life whose end is destruction because it is aimed at self, and it can be recognized in many forms.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 12 uses katalambano twice, and it is the heart of the verse's play: Paul presses on so that he may seize that for which he was himself seized by Christ Jesus. The verb means to lay hold of, to overtake or to grasp, and it appears in John 1:5 for the darkness not overcoming the light. Paul's chase is the answer to a prior capture. The verb teleioo, made perfect, and the adjective teleios, mature or complete, in verse 15 belong to one family. So Paul says, in effect, I have not been perfected, but let all who are perfect think this way. The word can mean full grown, as in 1 Corinthians 2:6 and Ephesians 4:13, and the play is that the mature are the ones who know they have not arrived.

The pair of participles in verse 13, epilanthanomenos, forgetting, and epekteinomenos, stretching out, are vivid. The second pictures a runner leaning forward with the whole body, reaching toward the line. The word skopos, translated goal, is the mark one fixes the eye on. Paul adds the phrase ano klesis, the upward call, which may point to the summons from above or the summons to the place above. The BSB renders it as heavenly calling.

In verse 15 the verb phroneo, to think or set the mind, begins a vocabulary that runs through the whole letter. The mind of Christ in 2:5, being like-minded in 2:2, the earthly mind of verse 19, and the shared mind of 4:2 are all this same verb. Verse 16 uses stoicheo, to walk in line, in step, a marching word. Verse 17 uses symmimetes, fellow imitator, and typos, pattern or mold, and skopeo, to watch closely. The imitation is not of a personality but of a shape of life.

Verse 19 turns on telos, end, and apoleia, destruction, set against the telos of verse 14 where the runner reaches the goal. Koilia, belly, stands for appetites generally. In verse 20 politeuma is a commonwealth, a body of citizens, and the verb apekdechomai, eagerly await, is a strong one, used of waiting for the revelation in Romans 8:19 and 8:23 and for Christ in Hebrews 9:28. Verse 21 gives metaschematizo, to change the outward form, with symmorphon, conformed in shape, and the body of our tapeinosis, humiliation, which is a cousin of the verb Christ used of Himself in 2:8, He humbled Himself. The power at work is energeia, the same root as the work of God in 2:13.

typology.fulfillment: Abraham left a known country for one God would show him, Genesis 12:1, and Hebrews 11:13 to 16 says the patriarchs confessed they were strangers and exiles because they were seeking a better, heavenly country. Philippians takes that same pilgrim identity and names its destination, a commonwealth in heaven. The escalation is that the pilgrims no longer have only a promise from afar; they have a Savior who has gone ahead and who is coming. The type falls short because the patriarchs never received what they sought in their lifetimes, while believers have the firstfruits of the Spirit now, Romans 8:23.

Israel was a nation constituted by God with laws, a land and a king, and Ephesians 2:12 speaks of Gentiles once being alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. Philippians says believers belong to a commonwealth in heaven, so the pattern of a people ruled by God is extended beyond one ethnic nation to all who are in Christ, Ephesians 2:19. The king of the new commonwealth is Christ Himself. The type falls short because Israel's land and borders were earthly and shared with others, whereas this homeland is secured by the resurrection, Colossians 3:1 to 4.

In Leviticus 23:10 the first sheaf of the harvest was brought to the priest as a pledge of the harvest to come. Paul says Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and Philippians 3:21 promises that His glorious body is the pattern of the harvest. The correspondence is exact because the first sheaf was of the same kind as the rest. It falls short because the grain sheaf was an offering for the crop, while Christ is both the offering and the head of those raised with Him.

Israel in the wilderness looked back at Egypt's food and asked to return, Numbers 11:5 and 14:3 to 4. Paul's forgetting what is behind is the opposite stance, a pilgrim who will not let the past pull back. Lot's wife is a warning of the same kind, Luke 17:32. Christ is the one who set His face toward the end of the road, Luke 9:51, and Hebrews 12:1 to 2 says to run looking to Him. The type is a contrast type: it shows what the runner must not do, and it falls short as a pattern because the wilderness generation never entered the land.

study.christ:
Christ stands at three points of this passage: before the race, at its end, and as its pattern. Before the race, because Paul says he is pressing on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of him. The pursuit is a reply to a prior act. Christ laid hold of Paul on the road to Damascus and has not let go, and the runner runs from that claim and not toward it. This answers the fear that spiritual effort is a way of earning. It is the response of one already seized, as 1 Corinthians 15:10 says of grace.

Christ is also the end of the race. The prize is the upward call in Christ Jesus, and the Savior who is awaited from heaven is the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul has already said in chapter 1 that to depart and be with Christ is far better, 1:23, and in verse 8 of this chapter that he counts all things loss to gain Him. The goal is a person. Hebrews 12:2 names Him the author and perfecter of faith and bids runners fix their eyes on Him.

He is the pattern as well. His glorious body is the model of what ours will be, as Paul says, and in Luke 24:39 and John 20:27 the risen Lord invites touch and shows wounds, which tells us that glory does not erase the body. It is a real body raised. Romans 8:29 says believers are predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son, and 1 Corinthians 15:49 says we will bear the likeness of the heavenly man. The same Christ who emptied Himself in 2:7 to 8 is the one who is glorified in 2:9, and this passage says that humility and glory will be the story of His people too, since the body of lowliness will be changed.

The power that does it is His. The power that enables Him to bring everything under His control is the working of the same strength that raised Him, Ephesians 1:19 to 20, and Psalm 8:6, as 1 Corinthians 15:27 reads it, says that everything has been put under His feet. The resurrection of believers is therefore not a hope grounded in their effort but in His reign.
study.god:
The first thing this passage says about God is that He calls. The prize is attached to a calling from above, and the initiative lies with God from start to finish. He lays hold before the runner begins, He calls the runner upward, and He is the one who will bring the end about. This is the same pattern as Philippians 1:6, and it assures the believer that the race is not a gamble.

He is also the God who reveals. Verse 15 promises that if the mature think differently about some matter, God will make it clear to them. That is a gentle, patient picture. He does not shout at the hesitating but leads them. It makes room for believers who disagree on lesser points, so long as they walk on the same line, verse 16. God is therefore a teacher who is not in a hurry.

Then the passage shows His power. In verse 21 it is the power by which He subjects all things to Himself, and it is turned to the humble work of changing human bodies. The same power that governs the world is gentle enough to renew a worn-out body. Paul sets the body of lowliness beside the body of glory, and God is the one who does the changing. The doctrine is that creation is not discarded but renewed; He is a God who keeps matter and raises it. That is why the hope is for a transformed body and not an escape from the body, 2 Corinthians 5:1 to 4.

He is just, as the fate of the enemies shows. Their end is destruction, and Paul does not soften it. The tears he weeps are real, yet the verdict stands. The God of the passage is both the one who weeps through His servant and the one who judges, and neither cancels the other.

He is also faithful to a people far from home. A colony of citizens is not forgotten by the capital; the Savior is coming from there. For worship, this means that waiting is a form of trust. The church eagerly awaits, which is not passive but expectant, and the right response to such a God is steady standing with a lifted head.

crossReferences.note: Paul's race passage, with its call to run so as to take the prize and its crown that does not perish. It shows that the athletic image in Philippians is a settled habit of his thought, and that discipline in the race is the fruit of grace and not a rival to it.

Run with endurance the race set out for us, fixing our eyes on Jesus. The writer joins Paul's image with its direction: the runner does not look at the track behind or at other runners, but at the Lord who ran it first and now sits at God's right hand.

Paul says he has finished the race and awaits the crown of righteousness for all who love His appearing. It is the same race seen from the finish. The one who said in Philippians that he had not yet arrived now says he has, and the prize is shared with all who long for the Lord.

The patriarchs were strangers and exiles seeking a better country. This is the pilgrim background for the citizenship of verse 20, and it shows that heavenly citizenship has always been the hope of the people of God, not a late idea.

Gentiles are no longer strangers and foreigners but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household. It describes how the commonwealth is formed: by being brought near in Christ, so that believers belong first to Him and then to each other.

What is sown perishable is raised imperishable, in glory and in power. This is the long form of verse 21, and it explains what changing a lowly body into a glorious one means, as well as why the likeness of the heavenly man is promised.

When Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is. John says what Paul says, that the transformation happens at His appearing and that the pattern is Christ Himself. It adds that the sight of Him is part of the change.

We groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for the redemption of our bodies. It joins eager waiting to the body, as verses 20 and 21 do, and shows that the Spirit's firstfruits already given are a pledge of the full harvest.

Paul describes those who avoid persecution for the cross and boasts only in the cross of Christ. It gives a close parallel to the enemies of the cross in verses 18 and 19, and shows what is at stake when the cross is made optional.

Set your minds on things above, for your life is hidden with Christ in God. It is the counterpart to the earthly minds of verse 19. When Christ appears, believers appear with Him in glory, which is the same movement as verses 20 and 21.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with human beings at home in a garden, walking with God, and it ends with a city in which God dwells with His people. In between, the people of God are mostly on the road. Abraham left, Israel crossed a desert, the exiles were carried to Babylon and came back to a land that never quite became home. The sense of not yet arriving is built into the story, and Philippians 3:12 to 21 gives it its Christian form.

The fall is what turned minds toward earthly things, as verse 19 says, so that a belly becomes a god and shame becomes glory. The race of the believer is the long reversal of that, with the mind slowly set on what is above, Colossians 3:2. The cross is the center of it, which is why those who reject it are enemies. In Christ the pilgrim is told to forget the road behind, since the old way has ended, and to stretch toward what is ahead.

The body has a place in the story from the beginning. God made humans out of the ground and called them very good, Genesis 1:31, and death entered with sin. Salvation is therefore not freedom from bodies but a rescue of bodies. The risen Christ is the first example, and verse 21 says His people will be changed to match. That is why Paul can speak of redemption as the redemption of our bodies, Romans 8:23, and why creation itself waits in eager expectation, Romans 8:19.

The destination is the new creation. Isaiah 65:17 promised new heavens and a new earth, and 2 Peter 3:13 says righteousness dwells there. Revelation 21:2 pictures the holy city coming down from heaven, so the commonwealth that now sits in heaven comes to earth. The citizens do not leave the world to go to heaven; heaven arrives where they are, and the Savior who was awaited from heaven dwells with them. The end of the race is a home.

quiz.q: What does Paul admit about himself in verses 12 and 13?

options.text: That he has not yet arrived or been made perfect, but presses on.
options.note: Verses 12 to 13 confess he has not yet obtained it and still strains ahead.

options.text: That he has already reached full perfection.
options.note: He explicitly denies this and keeps pressing on.

options.text: That he has given up trying altogether.
options.note: The opposite: he strains forward like a runner.

options.text: That the goal does not really matter.
options.note: He presses on toward the goal to win the prize.

quiz.q: What is the prize Paul runs toward?

options.text: The prize of God's heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.
options.note: Verse 14 names the goal as God's upward call in Christ.

options.text: Wealth and recognition in this life.
options.note: The prize is heavenly, not earthly reward.

options.text: A reward he earns as wages for his effort.
options.note: It is God's calling received at the finish, grounded in Christ's grasp of him, not wages.

options.text: Freedom from ever having to serve.
options.note: The prize is life with Christ, not escape from service.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the enemies of the cross?

options.text: Their god is their belly, their glory is in shame, their minds on earthly things.
options.note: Verse 19 describes their appetite-driven, earthbound life headed for destruction.

options.text: As harmless people who simply disagree politely.
options.note: Paul weeps over them; their end is destruction, not a minor disagreement.

options.text: As those who set their minds on heavenly things.
options.note: The opposite: their minds are set on earthly things.

options.text: As faithful examples to imitate.
options.note: They are the pattern to avoid, unlike the example Paul sets.

quiz.q: Where does Paul say the believer's true citizenship is?

options.text: In heaven, from which we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.
options.note: Verse 20 locates our citizenship in heaven and awaits Christ from there.

options.text: In Rome, under the authority of Caesar.
options.note: The pointed contrast is that our commonwealth is heaven, not Rome.

options.text: Wherever we happen to feel most at home.
options.note: Paul names a definite homeland, heaven, ruled by Christ.

options.text: Nowhere; believers belong to no kingdom.
options.note: We belong to a heavenly commonwealth with Jesus as Lord.

quiz.q: What will the Savior do for believers when He comes?

options.text: Transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.
options.note: Verse 21 promises the transformation of our bodies by Christ's power.

options.text: Free our souls from bodies forever.
options.note: The hope is transformed bodies, not escape from the body.

options.text: Leave our bodies unchanged.
options.note: He will transform them to be like His glorious body.

options.text: Reward only those who earned it by works.
options.note: The transformation is Christ's gift by His power, for His people.

questions: Paul refused to coast, saying I press on. Where in your walk with Christ have you settled for coasting instead of pursuing?
Paul forgot what was behind to strain toward what is ahead. What past failure or success is holding you back from pressing forward with Christ?
Paul wept over those whose minds were set on earthly things. Where are your own appetites and comforts in danger of becoming your god?
Your true citizenship is in heaven. How would remembering that you are a colony of heaven change how you live in your city this week?
The Savior is coming to transform your lowly body into glory. How does that certain hope help you stand firm when life feels weak and small?

translationNotes.note: Press on renders dioko, to pursue or chase hard; Paul denies having arrived while affirming strenuous, grace-driven pursuit, since Christ first took hold of him.
Citizenship translates politeuma, commonwealth; in a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, Paul declares the believer's true homeland is heaven, ruled by the Lord Jesus.
Transform renders metaschematizo, to refashion the outward form; the hope is the glorification of the body to match Christ's risen body, not escape from the body.
